analysis.one_liner: Requires the largest credit card issuers to let merchants route transactions over at least two competing payment networks.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Banking Committee: introduced with a bipartisan group of six senators, it got no committee or floor vote and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Big banks and the two dominant card networks, Visa and Mastercard, charge stores a fee on every credit card swipe and control which network processes it. The bill would force the largest issuers — those with over $100 billion in assets — to put at least two unaffiliated networks on every card and to stop penalizing stores that route purchases to the cheaper one. Merchants could then shop for the lowest fee, and backers argued savings would flow into lower prices. The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and never received any vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Merchants who accept credit cards — from big chains to local shops — would gain the right to route transactions over competing, often cheaper networks. Consumers would benefit indirectly if fee savings were passed through to prices; backers pointed to similar debit-card routing rules, which studies found lowered merchants' costs.

how_it_helps.text: Requires covered issuers — banks with more than $100 billion in assets — to enable each credit card to be processed on at least two networks, neither of which may be affiliated with the issuer or among the two largest networks by market share.

Bars issuers and networks from penalizing merchants for choosing how to route a transaction, including through volume thresholds or by locking merchants into security technology only the dominant networks can use.
Directs the Federal Reserve to publish a list of payment card networks that pose a national security risk or are owned or sponsored by a foreign state entity, and bars routing onto those networks.

analysis.who_pays: Visa and Mastercard, whose near-duopoly on large-issuer credit card routing would face real competition, and the largest banks, whose interchange (swipe) fee income funds card rewards programs and would likely shrink. Those banks argued that losses could show up as reduced rewards or higher card costs for consumers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Visa, Mastercard, and the biggest banks

drawbacks.text: The mandate covers only issuers with more than $100 billion in assets and exempts three-party systems like American Express and Discover entirely, so most of the card market would see no new competition.

The bill lets merchants route transactions to any network not flagged as a national-security risk, and critics — including the banks and networks — argued that shifting traffic onto smaller networks could mean less proven fraud protection and weaker rewards, since swipe fees pay for both.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential gain is real but indirect: merchants pay tens of billions a year in swipe fees, and comparable routing competition in the debit market demonstrably lowered those costs, with some of the savings historically reaching consumers as lower prices. The honest costs are uncertainty — rewards programs and fraud tools are funded by the same fees, so some households could see thinner perks — and a design gap: the mandate touches only the very largest issuers and skips Amex and Discover outright. On balance it is a targeted competition fix, not a sweeping overhaul, and its main cost falls on the networks and banks rather than on cardholders directly.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Banking Committee for the rest of the two-year Congress — no committee vote, no floor vote — and expired when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the Credit Card Competition Act of 2023 on June 7, 2023, joined by Senators Marshall, Welch, and Vance.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee the same day.
Five senators cosponsored the bill — three Republicans and two Democrats — but that was the last action on the bill in the record.
The bill never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or any other action for the remainder of the 118th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Visa, Mastercard, and the largest card-issuing banks keep the current routing rules — and the swipe fees that come with them — because the bill died without a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Visa, Mastercard, and large card-issuing banks

for.name: Dick Durbin
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, continuing his push for routing competition that he first won for debit cards in 2010.

for.name: Retail and merchant industry coalition
for.role: Retail trade groups representing stores that accept cards
for.what_they_did: Publicly campaigned for the bill, arguing routing choice would cut the swipe fees merchants pay on every credit sale.

against.name: Sherrod Brown
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee vote on the bill, leaving it pending in committee until the Congress ended.

against.name: Visa and Mastercard
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against the bill, arguing it would reduce security and push transactions onto less capable networks.

against.name: Large banks and banking trade groups
against.role: Major card-issuing banks and their trade associations
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill publicly, arguing that cutting swipe fees would shrink rewards programs and raise costs for cardholders.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan — a Democratic sponsor with three Republican and two Democratic cosponsors — and because the bill never came to a vote, the record shows no party-line split on its merits.

industries.note: The bill's carve-out for the two largest networks by market share is aimed squarely at their duopoly over large-issuer credit routing; letting merchants route elsewhere would erode their fee revenue. Their fees are embedded in nearly every card purchase, so their interest runs against merchants and shoppers here.

industries.industry: Large card-issuing banks (over $100 billion in assets)
industries.note: Interchange fees on credit transactions are a major revenue line, and the bill removes their ability to guarantee routing through the dominant network. Banks argued the fees fund rewards and fraud protection, so some of the cost could land back on cardholders.

industries.industry: Smaller payment networks and their partner banks
industries.note: Networks other than the two largest would suddenly be able to win transaction volume from the biggest issuers, which is the bill's entire point. More routing competition tends to push processing fees down.

The bill exempts three-party systems where the issuer is the network, leaving their closed-loop model untouched while their rivals face a mandate. They keep their fee structure with no new competition.

Stores pay a swipe fee on every credit sale and would gain the right to route to cheaper networks and to resist volume penalties and proprietary security lock-ins. Retailers were the bill's main outside champions.
